title: Regional fallback cost + SLA ladder: sales & incident messaging draft
content:
Purpose:
This working doc is a sales + incident-communications brief that translates technical fallback choices and multi-region architecture tradeoffs into concise, customer-facing language and a practical SLA / credit ladder. Use it when: sales is negotiating large reserved commitments, customer success needs an incident script, or marketing needs tight copy for reliability claims that are grounded in operational reality.

Audience:
- AEs and SEs preparing enterprise contracts
- Customer Success for incident comms and post-incident remediation
- Product Marketing for positioning against competitors

TL;DR (one-sentence summaries for rapid use):
- Multi-region active-active reduces outage risk but costs ~1.6–2.0x; suggest to pitch to customers with <1% tolerance for unavailability.
- Cost-conscious customers get predictable resilience via our fallback ladder (model variants + cached responses + latency-tiered routing) for ~1.05–1.2x cost.
- For enterprise customers we offer an SLA ladder: Bronze (single-region, 99.5%), Silver (multi-az, 99.9%), Gold (multi-region failover, 99.95% + runbook support).

Core messaging levers (how to explain technical options in plain language):
1) Active-active multi-region: "We keep your inference endpoints running in multiple geographic regions simultaneously so a regional outage has minimal customer impact. This gives the highest availability but requires reserved capacity across regions."
2) Tiered fallbacks: "If a region is impaired we automatically route to a lower-cost, compatible model variant or to a cached answer to keep your app responsive. Quality is slightly different in rare cases, but we never block user traffic."
3) Graceful degradation: "For heavy load or partial outages we prioritize critical routes and reduce non-essential features (e.g., long-form generation can be temporarily trimmed) to preserve latency for core flows."
4) Predictable credits: "SLA credits are calculated by region and feature — customers can choose a tighter SLA for higher critical routes."

Cost implications — quick numbers for sales conversations (ballpark):
- Single-region (on-demand hosted): baseline cost = 1.0x
- Multi-az within region (redundant infra, same region): +10–25% depending on autoscale buffer
- Active-active multi-region (reserved capacity in 2 regions): +60–100% relative to baseline (but reduces risk of total outage dramatically)
- Fallback ladder (model variants, prefix/KV caching, smaller reserve): +5–20% and reduces per-token cost during normal ops via caching benefits
Note: exact numbers depend on model family, quantization and burst profiles. Always offer to run a quick cost simulation from Redwood Optimize during contract talks.

SLA ladder and suggested contractual language (concise):
- Bronze (economy): 99.5% uptime SLA, regional failure tolerated, no guaranteed cross-region failover. "Bronze guarantees regional availability; credits apply for downtime beyond 0.5% monthly."
- Silver (business): 99.9% uptime, multi-az routing and automatic retries across zones, limited cross-region capacity for failover. "Silver adds multi-zone resilience and automated routing to reduce service interruption risk."
- Gold (enterprise): 99.95% uptime, active-active multi-region failover, dedicated runbook access and phone escalation, annual DR test. "Gold includes active-region failover and joint DR runbooks; credits and response timelines are commensurate with enterprise needs."

How to present degradation scenarios to customers (short scripts):
- Customer-facing (concise): "We detected increased latency from one region and shifted traffic automatically to a compatible region and faster cached responses. You may notice slightly shorter or more concise outputs in a small percentage of calls while we rehydrate model caches — core functionality remained available."
- Technical buyer (detailed): "During the incident we executed our fallback ladder: 1) routed traffic to secondary region via smart routing policy, 2) switched to natively-quantized model variant with compatible tokenizer for 15 minutes, 3) served cached completions for top 12 intents while KV caches warmed. Full model state restored after 22 minutes; post-incident report attached."
- Internal SE/CS playbook line: "If a customer asks whether full fidelity was preserved: say 'not always; we prioritized availability and latency for critical routes and documented any quality impact — details available in the incident report.' Offer to run post-incident quality audits against customer's eval suite."

Competitor callouts (short, non-combative):
- Vendor A: markets single-region high-availability only; may be cheaper short-term but lacks automated cross-region fallbacks.
- Vendor B: emphasizes active-active but charges high premiums for reserved cross-region capacity.
- Open-source self-host: variable reliability unless customer invests ops resources; Redwood trades that ops burden for predictable SLOs and observability.
Messaging angle: "We give predictable tradeoffs — cheaper fallback-first resilience for teams that prioritize cost, and robust multi-region options for teams that prioritize uninterrupted availability."

Incident narrative templates (email + Slack blurbs):
- Customer email (short): "We want to make you aware of an incident affecting inference latency in us-west-2 between 09:12–09:48 UTC. We automatically routed requests to us-east-1 and served cached responses to high-priority routes. Overall user-facing impact was minimized; we will follow up with a post-incident report in 48 hours. If you have a scheduled business-critical window, please flag and we will prioritize remediation and credits per your SLA."
- Internal Slack (ops -> cs): "Incident: us-west-2 increased error-rate. Action: routing to us-east-1 + quantized variant fallback. Impact: brief quality variance on long-gen routes. CS standby: notify top-ten customers with enterprise Gold SLA. Docs: link to live incident board and fallback config."

Sales objection responses (snappy):
- "Why not just multi-region everywhere?" -> "We recommend multi-region for mission-critical flows. For other workloads our fallback ladder is a lower-cost way to keep apps online with minimal visible impact — we can model both approaches for your traffic profile."
- "Will cached answers leak data?" -> "No — cache policies are configurable per-route and respect customer data retention and encryption settings. Sensitive routes can bypass caches or be tagged for short TTLs."
- "How do you measure quality loss?" -> "We use customer eval suites and can run pre/post comparisons whenever fallbacks activate; we surface regressions in Redwood Console and tie them to credits and remediation plans."

Playbook checklist for SEs during negotiation (quick steps):
1) Ask about RTO/RPO expectations and which routes are business-critical.
2) Run Redwood Optimize cost vs availability simulation and include numbers in the proposal.
3) Propose an SLA ladder aligned to their critical routes (Gold for payments/identity, Bronze for low-priority batch jobs).
4) Get agreement on incident cadence and DR test cadence (annual or quarterly).

Post-incident items to offer (customer recovery package):
- Full incident timeline and technical root cause analysis
- Quality regression audit on customer prompt set (free for Gold customers)
- 1:1 walkthrough with platform engineer to tune routes and caching TTLs
- Credits per agreed SLA ladder

Open questions / decisions for product and legal: (notes for internal follow-up)
- Default credit calculation for multi-region partial degradations (percent allocation per-route?)
- Standard wording for limited-quality fallbacks in contract annex (must avoid overpromising exact fidelity)
- Pricing SKU for "fallback-only" resilience (lower-cost add-on vs full multi-region)

Appendix — short examples of language to use in UI or one-pagers:
- "Automatic regional routing keeps apps online during localized failures."
- "Fallback ladder preserves latency-sensitive flows while gracefully reducing non-essential features."
- "Pick the SLA ladder that matches your business impact: Bronze (cost-savvy), Silver (balanced), Gold (mission critical)."

Status: draft — this doc is intentionally conversational and contains working numbers. Please add notes from pricing and legal on the open questions above.

[End of doc]
